{{Use dmy dates|date=February 2023}}
'''Alexander Coker''' (born 1969) was formerly a Chief Inspector of the [[Chemical Weapons]] team in [[Iraq]], while working for the United Nations Monitoring, Verification and Inspection Commission ([[UNMOVIC]]). Prior to that he held various other posts at UNMOVIC and had been seconded from the British Government to carry out work for UNMOVIC’s predecessor, the United Nations Special Commission ([[UNSCOM]]).<ref name=PalgraveMacmillan>[https://www.amazon.com/Search-Iraqs-Weapons-Destruction-Non-Proliferation/dp/1403942579 Graham S. Pearson, ''The Search for Iraq's Weapons of Mass Destruction: Inspection, Verification and Non-Proliferation'', Palgrave Macmillan, New York 2005, pages 139-141, 146.]</ref><ref>BBC Radio 4, ''Weapons Inspectors Uncovered'', Thursday 10 July 2003 (Radio 4 programme, 8pm).</ref>

He holds a Ph.D from [[King's College London]],<ref>[http://catalogue.ulrls.lon.ac.uk/search~S16/q?author=coker&title=kinetic+and+equilibrium+ Alexander Coker, ''University of London (Senate House) Theses, University of London Research Theses: Coker, Alexander'', 1995.]</ref> where he published work on the stability of particular chemical systems.<ref>{{cite journal | doi=10.1039/P29950000001 | title=Substituent effects leading to ultra-slow proton removal from an intramolecular hydrogen bond | date=1995 | last1=Coker | first1=Alex | last2=Hibbert | first2=Frank | journal=Journal of the Chemical Society, Perkin Transactions 2 | page=1 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | doi=10.1039/DT99400BX059 | title=Back cover | journal=Journal of the Chemical Society, Dalton Transactions | date=1994 | issue=15 | pages=X059 }}</ref>

It is believed Dr. Coker was a leading contributor to the chemical section of UNMOVIC’s working document on Iraq’s Unresolved Disarmament Issues<ref name=WorkingDocument>[https://www.un.org/Depts/unmovic/documents/6mar.pdf UNMOVIC Working Document, ''Unresolved Disarmament Issues - Iraq’s Proscribed Weapons Programmes'', 6 March 2003.]</ref> and to the revision of the list of [[dual-use]] chemical items subject to notification by Iraq, under the Export/Import Mechanism approved by [[United Nations Security Council Resolution 1051|Security Council Resolution 1051]].<ref>[https://www.casi.org.uk/info/unmovic1051l010601/chemical.pdf UNMOVIC, ''“Revised Annex II”: “Dual-Use” Chemicals of the “1051 Lists” of dual-use equipment'', UN document number S/2001/560, 1 June 2001.]</ref>

Under Dr. Coker’s leadership, what is now known to have been the last remnants of chemical weapons (artillery shells containing mustard gas) were destroyed at [[Al Muthanna]] State Establishment (Iraq's former chemical weapons facility) - the shells were apparently part of an old stock pile remaining from prior to the first [[Gulf War]].<ref name= PalgraveMacmillan/><ref name= WorkingDocument/><ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.nytimes.com/2003/02/13/world/threats-responses-weapons-sleuths-inspectors-begin-destroying-10-iraqi-mustard.html | newspaper=The New York Times | title=Threats And Responses: Weapons Sleuths; Inspectors Begin Destroying 10 Iraqi Mustard Gas Shells | date=13 February 2003 | first=Ian | last=Fisher | accessdate=14 February 2023}}</ref>

Dr. Coker is mentioned in the evidence of the [[Hutton Inquiry]] investigation into the circumstances surrounding the death of [[David Kelly (weapons expert)|Dr. David Kelly]]<ref>[http://www.the-hutton-inquiry.org.uk/content/com/com_4_0084.pdf The Hutton Enquiry Archives, ''Evidence - Files retrieved from Dr Kelly’s home computer: E-mail from Dr Kelly 9 July 03'', Inquiry File reference COM/4/0084.] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081121033753/http://www.the-hutton-inquiry.org.uk/content/com/com_4_0084.pdf |date=2008-11-21 }}</ref> and by the Verification Research, Training and Information Centre ([[VERTIC]]).<ref>[https://www.vertic.org/media/assets/TV114.pdf Jessica McLaughlin, ''Confidentiality and verification: the IAEA and OPCW'', Trust and Verify, May-June 2004 (Issue 114), page 11.]</ref>
